lessons.title: Subject and verb
lessons.tip: A sentence needs a subject (who or what) and a verb (the action or state). Put the subject first: “Maria runs.” “The dog sleeps.” Begin with a capital letter and end with a period.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (A1 descriptors)

lessons.title: Add an object
lessons.tip: Many sentences add an object, the person or thing that receives the action: “Sam eats an apple.” Keep the order subject, verb, object. English does not move the object to the front.

lessons.title: Commands and requests
lessons.tip: A command starts with the verb: “Open the door.” Add “please” to be polite: “Please open the door.” To say what not to do, start with “Don’t”: “Don’t run.”

lessons.title: Join with and, but, or
lessons.tip: Join ideas with a small word. Use “and” to add, “but” to show a difference, and “or” to give a choice: “I like tea and coffee.” “I like tea, but I don’t like coffee.” “Do you want tea or coffee?”

lessons.title: Do and does in questions
lessons.tip: To ask a yes/no question, start with “Do” or “Does.” Use “Does” with he, she and it: “Does she like tea?” Use “Do” with I, you, we and they: “Do you like tea?” After Do or Does, the main verb stays in its base form: like, not likes.

lessons.title: Past simple
lessons.tip: Use the past simple for finished actions at a known time: “I visited my aunt yesterday.” Regular verbs add -ed: work, worked. Many common verbs are irregular: go, went; see, saw; buy, bought. In questions and negatives use did + the base verb: “Did you see it?” “I didn’t see it.” Time words that go with it: yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (A2-B1 descriptors)

lessons.title: Present simple or present continuous
lessons.tip: Use the present simple for habits and facts: “She walks to work.” Use the present continuous for actions happening now or around now: “She is walking to work today.” The continuous uses am/is/are + verb-ing. Words like always, usually and every day go with the simple. Words like now, at the moment and today go with the continuous. Some verbs, such as know, like and want, are usually not used in the continuous.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (A2-B1 descriptors)

lessons.title: Will and going to
lessons.tip: Use going to for plans you have already made and for things you can see will happen: “I’m going to visit my uncle.” “Look at those clouds. It’s going to rain.” Use will for quick decisions, offers and predictions: “I’ll help you.” “I think it will be fun.” The short form is ’ll. Negative: won’t.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.tip: Use the comparative to compare two things: “This bag is cheaper than that one.” Short adjectives add -er (cheap, cheaper); longer ones use more (expensive, more expensive). Use the superlative for the top of three or more: “the cheapest,” “the most expensive.” Some are irregular: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst. Use “as … as” for equal things: “as big as.”
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (A2-B1 descriptors)

lessons.title: Can, should, must, have to
lessons.tip: Modal verbs add meaning. Can shows ability or permission: “I can swim.” Should gives advice: “You should rest.” Must shows a strong duty or a rule: “You must wear a seatbelt.” Have to is similar and is often used for rules from others: “I have to work on Saturday.” After a modal use the base verb with no to or -s: “She can swim,” not “She cans to swim.” Mustn’t means do not; don’t have to means it is not necessary.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (A2-B1 descriptors)

lessons.title: Countable and uncountable
lessons.tip: Countable nouns can be counted: one apple, two apples. Uncountable nouns cannot: water, rice, advice, information. Use many and a few with countable nouns; use much and a little with uncountable nouns. Use a lot of with both. In questions and negatives use any: “Do you have any milk?” In positive sentences use some: “I have some milk.” Words like advice and information are never plural.

CEFR Companion Volume (A2-B1 descriptors)

lessons.title: Prepositions of time and place
lessons.tip: For time: use at with clock times and night (at six, at night), on with days and dates (on Monday, on 5 May), and in with months, years, seasons and parts of the day (in July, in 2020, in the morning). For place: in a room or city, on a surface or street, at a point or event (at the bus stop, at the party). Learn common pairs as chunks: at home, on holiday, in bed, at work.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (A2-B1 descriptors)

lessons.title: Present perfect: since and for
lessons.tip: Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) for situations that began in the past and continue now, or for results that matter now. Use for with a length of time (for six years) and since with a starting point (since 2019). “I have lived here for six years” means I still live here. Words that go with it: ever, never, already, yet, just. Past participles: been, gone, done, seen, written, taken.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (B1-B2 descriptors)

lessons.title: Present perfect or past simple?
lessons.tip: Use the past simple for a finished time: “I saw that film last year.” Use the present perfect when the time is not given or still connects to now: “I have seen that film” (at some time in my life), “I’ve lost my keys” (I still don’t have them). Do not use the present perfect with finished time words such as yesterday, last week or in 2010. Ask “When?” and you will need the past simple.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (B1-B2 descriptors)

lessons.title: If sentences: real and unreal
lessons.tip: First conditional: if + present, will + base verb, for real possibilities: “If it rains, we’ll stay home.” Second conditional: if + past, would + base verb, for unreal or unlikely situations: “If I won the lottery, I would travel.” In the unreal case, use were for all persons in formal English: “If I were you, I’d apologize.” Do not use will in the if-part.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (B1-B2 descriptors)

lessons.title: The passive voice
lessons.tip: Use the passive when the action matters more than who did it, or when the doer is unknown: “The window was broken.” Form: be + past participle. Present: “English is spoken here.” Past: “The bridge was built in 1990.” Add by + doer only if it is useful: “The book was written by a student.” Only transitive verbs have a passive; you cannot say “It was happened.”

lessons.title: Relative clauses
lessons.tip: A relative clause adds information about a noun. Use who for people, which for things and that for either in defining clauses: “The woman who lives next door is a doctor.” “The book that I read was long.” Use where for places: “That is the cafe where we met.” Use commas around extra information, and use which, not that: “My car, which is old, still runs.” You can leave out who/which/that when it is the object: “The film (that) we saw was great.”

lessons.title: Reported speech
lessons.tip: When we report what someone said, the tense usually moves back one step: “I am tired” becomes She said (that) she was tired. Present simple becomes past simple; will becomes would; can becomes could. Pronouns and time words change too: “I will come tomorrow” becomes He said he would come the next day. For questions use if or the question word, and normal word order: “Where do you live?” becomes She asked where I lived.

lessons.title: Must, might and can’t
lessons.tip: Use modal verbs to say how sure you are. Must means you are almost certain it is true: “He must be tired; he worked all night.” Might or may means it is possible: “She might be at home.” Can’t means you are almost certain it is false: “That can’t be his coat; it is too small.” For the past use modal + have + past participle: “He must have left.” “She can’t have known.”

CEFR Companion Volume (B1-B2 descriptors)

lessons.title: Link ideas: although, however, despite
lessons.tip: Use linking words to connect contrasting ideas. Although, even though and while introduce a clause: “Although it was raining, we went out.” Despite and in spite of are followed by a noun or -ing: “Despite the rain, we went out.” However and nevertheless start a new sentence and take a comma: “It was raining. However, we went out.” Use because and so for reasons and results, and therefore for a formal result.

lessons.title: Inversion for emphasis
lessons.tip: After some negative or restrictive adverbials, English puts the auxiliary before the subject, like a question: “Never have I seen such a view.” “Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.” “Rarely does he complain.” “Hardly had we arrived when it began to rain.” This is formal and emphatic. Without an auxiliary, add do/does/did. Use it sparingly for effect. In conditionals, “Should you need help…” and “Had I known…” replace if.

CEFR Companion Volume (C1-C2 descriptors)

lessons.title: Hypotheticals, regrets and wishes
lessons.tip: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle, for unreal past situations: “If I had left earlier, I would have caught the train.” Mixed conditionals combine times: “If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.” Wish and if only express regret or desire: “I wish I knew the answer” (present), “I wish I had studied” (past), “I wish he would stop” (annoyance). After “would rather” and “it’s time” the past tense has present or future meaning: “It’s time we left.”
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (C1-C2 descriptors)

lessons.title: Past modals and hedging
lessons.tip: Past modals: should have + participle criticizes or regrets (“You should have called”); could have shows past possibility (“We could have won”); might have shows a past possibility you are unsure about; needn’t have means it was not necessary but you did it. lessons.title: Dense noun phrases
lessons.tip: Academic and professional English packs information into noun phrases. Nominalization turns verbs or adjectives into nouns: “decide” becomes “the decision,” “different” becomes “the difference.” “Prices rose sharply” can become “the sharp rise in prices.” Add modifiers before and after the noun: “a recent, widely discussed report on urban transport.” Balance: too many nouns in a row become heavy. Use a verb when the action matters more than the idea.

CEFR Companion Volume (C1-C2 descriptors)

lessons.title: Participle and reduced clauses
lessons.tip: Participle clauses add information compactly. Present participle for simultaneous or causal action: “Walking home, I met an old friend.” Past participle for passive meaning: “Written in 1920, the book is still read.” Perfect participle for an earlier action: “Having finished, she left.” The subject of the participle must be the subject of the main clause, or you create a misplaced modifier: “Walking home, the rain started” is wrong. Reduced relative clauses: “the man standing there.”

CEFR Companion Volume (C1-C2 descriptors)

lessons.title: Formal structures
lessons.tip: Formal English uses structures that casual speech avoids. The subjunctive appears after verbs of demand or suggestion: “She insisted that he be present.” “It is essential that every student complete the form.” “Were it not for your help, we would have failed.” Passive and impersonal forms keep a neutral tone: “It is suggested that…”, “Attention is drawn to…” Use these in letters, reports and rules; they sound stiff in friendly chat.

lessons.title: Register: formal and informal
lessons.tip: Register is the level of formality. Compare two messages: a formal letter says “I am writing to enquire whether the position remains open”; a chat says “just checking if the job’s still going.” Informal English uses contractions, phrasal verbs (find out, put up with), ellipsis and slang; formal English prefers full forms, single verbs of Latin origin (discover, tolerate), precise vocabulary and longer sentences. Match the register to audience and purpose; mixing registers sounds awkward.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (C1-C2 descriptors)

lessons.title: Cohesion across sentences
lessons.tip: Cohesion is what makes sentences hold together. Use reference (this, that, the former), substitution (do so, one) and ellipsis (leaving out repeated words: “Some agreed; others did not”). Discourse markers signal structure: in the first place, moreover, by contrast, in sum. Put known information first and new information last so each sentence builds on the one before. Avoid starting every sentence the same way. Read your paragraph aloud: if you stumble, a link is missing.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)
CEFR Companion Volume (C1-C2 descriptors)
